strengths: Identifies and empirically documents an interesting phenomenon: reasoning uncertainty/errors are concentrated in a small subset of high-entropy tokens (Fig. 1), which is intuitive and reasonably well supported by the entropy histograms.

The proposed intervention (selective CFG only at high-entropy positions, plus KV-cache-reusing negative-prompt injection) is simple, training-free, and computationally cheap, which is an attractive practical property.
Experiments span a wide range of model sizes (8B/14B/32B), both base and reasoning variants, and three task categories (general, coding, math/STEM), giving broad (if not deep) coverage.

Useful diagnostic analyses: the entropy-partitioned analysis of which tokens vanilla CFG can/cannot change (Fig. 5), word-cloud comparisons, and a qualitative case study help build an intuitive narrative for why the method works.
Ablations on entropy threshold τ, CFG strength ω, and negative-prompt choice are included, adding some robustness analysis to the design choices.
weaknesses: The entropy threshold τ is swept over many values (0.1–2.0) directly on the test benchmarks (Tables 1 and 2), and the headline numbers quoted in the abstract/introduction (e.g., +1.35% on Qwen3-8B-Base, +5% on AIME2024 for Qwen3-32B) correspond to whichever τ happened to perform best per model/setting. No principled, held-out procedure for selecting τ prospectively is described, so it is unclear how a practitioner would choose τ without first evaluating on the test set—this materially undermines the soundness of the claimed gains and reproducibility of the specific reported numbers.

Related to the above, in Table 2 the best-performing τ differs by column/task even within the same model, and the bolded 'best' entries are effectively selected post hoc per metric, which further inflates the apparent consistency of gains relative to a single, fixed operating point.

Most benchmark results (WinoGrande, MMLU-Pro, GPQA-Diamond, MATH500, HumanEval(+), LiveCodeBench) appear to be single greedy-decoding runs with no variance/significance reporting, while AIME2024 is averaged over only 8 seeds; given many reported gains are on the order of 1–2 points, the lack of variance estimates makes it hard to assess whether improvements are statistically meaningful, especially on small test sets (e.g., HumanEval has only 164 problems).

The Vanilla CFG baseline (VC) underperforms even Direct Inference in almost all settings, which is somewhat surprising given CFG's reported benefits elsewhere; it is not clear whether ω was tuned fairly/separately for the VC baseline versus the proposed method, raising concerns about baseline fairness.

The empirical comparison is limited to only two baselines (Direct Inference and Vanilla CFG) on a single model family (Qwen3); there is no comparison to other test-time intervention or entropy-guided methods mentioned in the related work (e.g., high-entropy RL token selection, token pruning/skipping approaches), nor to other model families, limiting evidence for generality of the claims.

The practical simplicity claimed by the method ('minimal intervention') is undercut by the need to tune both τ and ω per model/task for good performance, which is not trivial to do without test-set access, and the paper does not provide clear guidance or a default recipe for new models/tasks.

strengths: Simple, training-free, practical intervention that targets only high-entropy tokens, with a lightweight KV-cache-reuse mechanism to avoid the cost of maintaining a separate unconditional branch for CFG.

Broad empirical coverage: multiple model families/sizes (Qwen3-8B/14B/32B, DeepSeek-R1-7B, Ling-mini-2.0), multiple task domains (general, coding, STEM), both greedy and stochastic decoding, and an extension to vision-language spatial reasoning benchmarks, showing the idea generalizes beyond a narrow setting.

Reasonably thorough ablations (entropy threshold τ, CFG strength ω, choice/semantics of negative prompt) and mechanistic analyses (entropy-conditioned CFG-success histogram in Fig. 4, word-cloud shift, qualitative case study) that provide some intuition for why the method works.

Comparisons against relevant baselines and SOTA test-time-scaling/efficiency methods (TALE, NoThinking, Dynasor, DEER, CGRS) and against vanilla CFG and contrastive decoding, situating the contribution within the existing landscape.

Efficiency claims are supported with latency measurements showing negligible or even reduced overhead relative to direct inference, addressing a central motivation of the paper (avoiding costly test-time scaling).
weaknesses: The entropy threshold τ is swept over multiple values per dataset/model in Table 1 and 2, and the headline numbers (e.g., +9.28% average, +11.25% AIME2024) appear to correspond to whichever τ performs best on that specific test set, rather than a single value chosen via a held-out validation procedure; the paper only asserts (without demonstrating) that τ could be tuned via cross-validation on a separate split, so the reported gains likely reflect a degree of test-set-optimized hyperparameter selection that inflates apparent effectiveness and undermines reproducibility of the exact numbers.

No variance/confidence intervals are reported for the main Table 1 results (only AIME2024 in Table 2 uses multiple runs), so it is unclear how much of the observed gains and the VC-underperforms-DI phenomena are due to noise versus a genuine effect, especially given greedy decoding is deterministic but single-seed.

The theoretical connection to classifier-free guidance is loose: unlike diffusion CFG, which trains an explicit null/unconditional branch, MTI substitutes a heuristic 2-word negative prompt ("OUTPUT ERROR") reused from the conditional KV cache; this is closer to ad hoc contrastive/negative prompting than a principled approximation of an unconditional distribution, and the paper does not rigorously justify why this construction faithfully approximates CFG's intended effect beyond empirical trial-and-error over prompt choices (Fig. 3c, Table 8).

The core empirical motivation (a few high-entropy tokens drive errors) substantially overlaps with existing high-entropy-token literature already cited (e.g., Wang et al. 2025's 'high-entropy minority tokens drive RL'), and the paper does not clearly delineate what is conceptually new versus applying a known observation to a new training-free intervention.

Absolute token entropy (unnormalized, vocabulary/temperature dependent) is used as the intervention trigger with a fixed threshold τ that varies substantially in optimal value across models/datasets/decoding settings (e.g., different best τ for DeepSeek-R1-7B vs. Qwen3-32B vs. VLM setting), raising doubts about the claimed robustness/insensitivity to τ and about practical deployment without per-task tuning.

Some counterintuitive results are underexplained, e.g., vanilla CFG (VC) with the same negative prompt sometimes underperforms direct inference by a large margin (e.g., Qwen3-32B DI 88.67 vs VC 86.02, AIME2024 Qwen3-32B DI 79.58 vs VC 72.92), which is attributed to blanket intervention harming low-entropy tokens, but this explanation is not independently verified against alternative causes such as suboptimal ω for VC specifically.
